blocks.text: Iterative prompting is the practice of refining a specific output across several turns of a live conversation, giving targeted feedback on what to change, rather than trying to get a perfect result from a single initial prompt.

This topic covers how iterative prompting differs from the prompt lifecycle covered earlier in this course, what makes follow-up feedback effective, how conversation history supports each new iteration, and recognizing when an output has genuinely converged and iteration should stop.
1. What Iterative Prompting Means
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473225769-513142953.png

Iterative prompting treats a conversation as a sequence of refinement steps, an initial output, specific feedback on what to change, a revised output, more feedback, continuing until the result actually meets the need.
2. Iterative Prompting vs the Prompt Lifecycle

blocks.alt: Iterative Prompting vs the Prompt Lifecycle
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473225770-952820677.png

The earlier Prompt Lifecycle topic covered a developer refining a reusable prompt template over time, informed by testing and production monitoring, iterative prompting is a different scope entirely, a user refining one specific output, live, within a single ongoing conversation.
3. Follow-Up Refinement Turns
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473225770-480455046.png

Each iteration is a natural conversational turn, the user reviews the current output, identifies specifically what does or does not work, and asks for a targeted change, rather than restarting from scratch with an entirely new prompt each time.

code.content:
Turn 1: "Write a product description for this water bottle."
Turn 2: "Make the second paragraph shorter and mention the price."
Turn 3: "Good, now make the tone a bit more casual."

blocks.text: 4. What Makes Follow-Up Feedback Effective
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473225771-692653682.png

This connects directly to the specificity principle covered throughout this course, "make it better" gives the model very little to actually act on, "shorten the second paragraph and mention the price" identifies exactly what needs to change, producing a far more targeted revision.

blocks.text: 5. Why Conversation History Helps Each Iteration

blocks.alt: Why Conversation History Helps Each Iteration
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473225771-705788314.png

Because each new turn happens within an ongoing conversation, the model has direct access to the original output and every piece of feedback given so far, this connects to the system versus user prompt structure covered in an earlier topic, this accumulated context is what lets a brief follow-up like "shorten it" work without needing to restate the entire original request.

blocks.title: This is a genuine practical advantage of chat based interfaces
blocks.content: A single-shot prompt has to be complete and self-contained, an iterative conversation lets a user refine incrementally, leaning on the model access to everything said earlier in that same conversation.

blocks.text: 6. Knowing When to Stop Iterating
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473225771-917776815.png

Iteration should stop once the output genuinely satisfies the actual requirement, continuing to iterate past that point, chasing marginal improvements with no real remaining problem, tends to waste time without meaningfully improving the result.
7. Iterative Prompting vs Self-Critique and Reflection

Self-critique and reflection, both covered in earlier topics, are largely automated, the model critiques or reflects on its own work with limited or no human involvement in between, iterative prompting is explicitly human-in-the-loop, a person reviews each output and decides what specific feedback to give next.
8. Common Iteration Patterns
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473226096-1472040.png

Iteration typically follows one of a few recognizable patterns, narrowing, adding a more specific constraint to an already reasonable output, expanding, asking for more detail or depth, or redirecting, realizing the current direction is not right and asking for a genuinely different approach.
9. Iterative Prompting in Practice

This pattern shows up constantly in real usage, writing assistance, code review conversations, and design brainstorming all typically involve several rounds of targeted feedback rather than a single perfect prompt producing a final result immediately.
Worked Example

A writer asks a model for a blog post introduction, the first draft is reasonable but too formal for the intended audience, they respond "make this more conversational and add a question to hook the reader," the model revises accordingly.

A further round, "the hook question is good, but shorten the whole thing by half," produces a final version that satisfies the actual need, reached through three brief, targeted turns rather than trying to specify every requirement perfectly in the very first prompt.
Common Mistakes

items: Giving vague follow-up feedback like make it better instead of naming the specific change needed
Continuing to iterate past the point where the output already genuinely satisfies the actual requirement
Starting an entirely new conversation for each refinement instead of continuing the existing one and losing valuable context
Confusing iterative prompting, a live, human-in-the-loop process, with the largely automated self-critique or reflection techniques

blocks.text: Practice

Ask a model for an initial draft of something, a short piece of writing or a piece of code, then give two or three rounds of specific, targeted feedback, and notice how much more efficient this feels compared to trying to specify every requirement in a single upfront prompt.
Key Takeaway

Iterative prompting refines a specific output across several conversation turns through targeted, specific feedback, leaning on the accumulated conversation history so each new turn does not need to restate everything from scratch, and it works best when a person recognizes exactly when the output has genuinely converged and iteration can stop.
